items.claim: Appending a fake static extension to a path and getting a 200 is not web cache deception on its own; the finding requires the cached body to contain the requesting user's data, because a static-file miss that returns the application's normal 404 page caches only public content.
items.disproof: The rule is wrong when the origin serves the same dynamic content for any path that merely looks static — a single-page app shell, a catch-all rewrite, or a server that ignores unknown extensions — in which case the cached object is the authenticated user's page and the deception is real even though nothing about the path was ever a static file.

items.claim: Web cache deception is proved by a second request for the same URL, made with a different or absent session, returning the first client's data — the shared cached object is the evidence, not the fact that the URL contains an extension.
items.disproof: The claim is false when the cache varies on a header or cookie and the second client sends a different one, in which case a different object is legitimately served and the deception has not occurred; the test must hold the cache-key components constant while changing only the identity.

items.claim: A cached 404 is not an information leak: the default edge TTL applied to 404 and 410 responses is minutes long and the cached object is the origin's error page, so caching it produces at most a stale missing page and no disclosure of the requester's data.
items.disproof: The rule is wrong when the origin's own 404 handler renders user-specific content — a signed-in shell, an internal error detail, a per-user tenant name — or when the edge caches a 404 for a path that was genuinely private, in which case the cached object does carry data and the deception holds despite the status code.

items.claim: An origin-side rule that refuses to serve responses for paths ending in a static extension closes the naive deception payload but not the same attack through a catch-all route, because a rewrite that maps every unmatched path to the application handler still returns the user's page under a cacheable URL.
items.disproof: The rule is false when the application genuinely has no catch-all and returns its own 404 for unknown static-looking paths, or when the cache key itself includes the path in a way that cannot be reused — then the naive payload and its variants both fail and the allowlist holds.

items.claim: The observation that distinguishes cache deception from ordinary caching is a cache HIT served for a URL that the origin never had as a static file, since a normal cache entry is only ever created for a resource the origin actually produced.
items.disproof: The claim is false when the origin does have a matching static file and the deception succeeded on a different URL form, or when the edge reports the HIT for a request whose cache lookup was actually a revalidation rather than a stored object; the X-Cache/AGE header values and the file inventory must both be captured before treating the HIT as evidence.
